title: Abbas ibn Firnas and the Dream of Flight
summary: The life of Abbas ibn Firnas, a ninth-century inventor in Cordoba who built clever machines and tried to glide through the air with homemade wings.
poll: Trying something new is worth it, even if it does not work the first time.

versions.title: The Man Who Tried to Fly
versions.text:
Long ago, a man named Abbas ibn Firnas lived in Cordoba. Cordoba is a city in Spain. He lived more than a thousand years ago.

Abbas was an inventor. He made new things. He made a clock that ran on water. He found a way to cut hard, clear rock. He made a room that looked like the sky at night.

Abbas liked to watch birds. He had a big dream. He wanted to fly!

So he made a pair of wings. He used wood and silk. He put lots of feathers on them.

One day, he went up a high hill. He held out his arms. Then he jumped! He did not drop like a stone. He went a long way through the air. He could glide.

Then it was time to land. He came down hard. He hurt his back. Why? He said he forgot to add a tail. Birds use a tail to slow down.

Abbas did not fly far. But he was brave. He tried. Now a big hole on the Moon has his name.

More than a millennium ago, a man named Abbas ibn Firnas resided within the city of Cordoba, situated in what constitutes present-day Spain. During the ninth century, Cordoba ranked among the most influential cities anywhere in the world, celebrated extensively for its enormous libraries, its distinguished scholars, and its remarkable scientific discoveries. Abbas himself emerged as one of its most imaginative and versatile intellectuals.

Abbas functioned simultaneously as an inventor, a poet, and a musician who derived particular satisfaction from solving practical, mechanical problems. He constructed an elaborate clock that employed flowing water to measure time with reasonable accuracy. He also developed an innovative technique for cutting a hard, transparent mineral called crystal. Local craftspeople no longer needed to transport it laboriously all the way to Egypt merely to have it properly shaped. He even designed an extraordinary chamber that imitated the appearance of the nocturnal sky, complete with artificial stars, simulated clouds, and intermittent flashes resembling lightning that thoroughly astonished his numerous visitors.

Abbas additionally harbored a profound fascination with the movement of birds. He frequently wondered how such creatures managed to remain aloft within the air for such extended durations. He gradually began imagining the possibility of flying himself through the sky.

To rigorously test his theoretical conviction, he constructed an elaborate pair of wings. He meticulously assembled a lightweight wooden frame, subsequently covered it entirely with silk fabric, and painstakingly attached numerous individual feathers across its surface.

On one particularly memorable occasion, when he had already attained considerable age, he ascended an elevated hill overlooking the city while a curious, sizable crowd gathered below to observe the spectacle. He extended his elaborate wings and launched himself boldly into the open air. Rather than plummeting directly downward, he traveled a genuinely considerable distance, since his wings permitted him to glide smoothly through the atmosphere.

Landing, however, proved to constitute a serious and painful difficulty, since he descended far too rapidly and consequently injured his back upon impact. Afterward, he explained candidly that he had neglected entirely to construct a tail, an appendage which birds characteristically employ to reduce their velocity before executing a landing.

The overwhelming majority of what we presently know regarding this remarkable flight originates from a historian named al-Maqqari, who described the episode centuries afterward while drawing upon earlier written sources. Consequently, certain details of the narrative may not prove entirely accurate, although historians generally concur that Abbas constituted a genuine, respected inventor of considerable accomplishment.

Although Abbas ultimately traveled only a modest distance through the air, he nevertheless demonstrated tremendous personal courage by attempting something that nobody within his immediate surroundings had previously dared to attempt. His legacy persists prominently even today, since a crater situated upon the Moon and a bridge spanning the river in Cordoba both continue carrying his name, perpetually reminding people everywhere that scientific progress frequently originates from a single daring, uncertain experiment.

wrong.A: A hard landing does not clean anything.
wrong.C: Stretching is not a result of a crash.
wrong.D: Nothing in the sentence is covered.

questions.stem: According to Abbas, what caused his hard landing?
options: The crowd was too noisy and made him lose focus.
The hill was not high enough.
The silk was torn.
His wings had no tail to slow him down.
questions.why: He explained that he forgot to make a tail, which birds use to slow down before landing.

wrong.A: The crowd only watched; it did not cause the landing.
wrong.B: He glided a long way, so the hill was high enough.
wrong.C: The article does not say the silk tore.

questions.stem: What does the room that looked like the night sky suggest about Abbas?
options: He was afraid of the dark and wanted a bright room.
He was curious about the sky and nature.
He did not like stars.
He wanted to live underground.
questions.why: Building a room with stars, clouds, and lightning shows he was very interested in the sky.

wrong.A: The article does not suggest fear.
wrong.C: He put stars in his room, so he must have liked them.
wrong.D: Nothing suggests he wanted to live underground.

questions.stem: What lesson might later inventors learn from Abbas's flight?
options: Flying machines need a way to control and slow down.
People should never try to fly.
Feathers are better than wood.
Hills are too dangerous to climb.
questions.why: Abbas could glide but could not land safely without a tail, so control and slowing down matter.

wrong.B: The article praises his courage for trying.
wrong.C: He used both wood and feathers; the article does not rank them.
wrong.D: The problem was the landing, not climbing the hill.

questions.stem: How does the author organize the article?
options: By comparing Abbas with the modern pilots who fly airplanes today
By listing problems in Cordoba and their solutions
By describing Abbas's life and inventions, then his flight, then how he is remembered
By explaining how birds fly, step by step, from takeoff to landing
questions.why: The article moves from his city and inventions, to the wings and the flight, to the honors that carry his name.

wrong.B: The article is a life story, not a list of city problems.
wrong.D: Birds are mentioned, but the article does not explain how they fly step by step.

MID.prompt: Explain why Abbas ibn Firnas is still remembered today. Use at least two details from the article to support your answer.
checklist: I gave a clear answer to the question.
I supported my answer with at least two details from the article.
I explained how each detail shows why he is remembered.
MID.modelAnswer: Abbas ibn Firnas is still remembered today because he was a brave inventor who tried something no one around him had ever attempted. He built a frame covered in silk and feathers so he could glide through the air, showing incredible courage even as an old man. He is remembered so well that a crater on the Moon and a bridge in Cordoba now carry his name, proving that people still honor his daring idea centuries later.

keyWords.definition: a person who has studied a subject deeply and gained great knowledge
keyWords.example: The scholar translated ancient texts about medicine.

keyWords.definition: to copy the way something looks, sounds, or acts
keyWords.example: Parrots can imitate the voices of people around them.

keyWords.definition: to move smoothly through the air, held up by wings instead of power
keyWords.example: Hang-gliders glide above the cliffs for many minutes.

keyWords.definition: a person who studies and writes about the past
keyWords.example: The historian used old letters to learn how people lived.

keyWords.definition: something a person leaves behind that is remembered after they are gone
keyWords.example: The teacher's legacy is the library she started in our town.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Abbas ibn Firnas proved that humans could fly just as well and as far as birds do.
Al-Maqqari was the most important historian of Cordoba.
Cordoba's libraries were larger than any others in the world during the ninth century.
Abbas ibn Firnas was a creative inventor whose daring flight attempt left a lasting legacy.
questions.why: The article presents his inventions, his brave but imperfect glide, and the ways he is honored today.

wrong.A: He glided a distance but landed badly; the article does not say he flew as well as birds.
wrong.B: Al-Maqqari is a supporting detail about the source of the story.
wrong.C: The libraries are background, and no comparison is made.

questions.stem: According to the article, who wrote down most of what we know about the flight?
options: Abbas himself
A historian named al-Maqqari
A crowd of scholars
The builders of the bridge in Cordoba
questions.why: The article states that most of what we know comes from the historian al-Maqqari, who wrote centuries later.

wrong.A: The article does not say Abbas wrote the account.
wrong.C: A crowd watched, but the account comes from al-Maqqari.
wrong.D: The bridge honors Abbas; its builders did not record the flight.

questions.stem: What made Abbas's sky room remarkable?
options: It was built on the Moon.
It was made entirely of cut crystal from Egypt.
It imitated stars, clouds, and lightning.
It was used to measure time.
questions.why: The article describes a room that imitated the night sky with stars, clouds, and flashes of lightning.

wrong.A: Only a crater on the Moon is named after him.
wrong.D: The water clock measured time, not the room.

questions.stem: The article says some details 'may not be completely accurate.' Why does the author include this statement?
options: To show that the account was written long after the event
To prove that Abbas never really existed at all
To criticize the people who watched the flight
To explain the method for cutting crystal
questions.why: The author warns readers that the story was written centuries later from older sources, so some details are uncertain.

wrong.B: The article treats Abbas as a real, respected inventor.
wrong.D: Crystal-cutting is unrelated to this statement.

questions.stem: What does the word legacy mean in the final paragraph?
options: A type of flying machine
Something for which a person is remembered
A building where scholars study
A sudden, dangerous fall
questions.why: His legacy is shown by the crater and bridge named after him, which keep his memory alive.

wrong.A: The wings were his machine; legacy refers to how he is remembered.
wrong.C: Libraries and schools are not what legacy means here.
wrong.D: His fall is part of the story, but legacy refers to lasting influence.

questions.stem: Why did crystal-cutting in Cordoba matter to local craftspeople?
options: It made crystal disappear completely from Spain.
It forced them to move to Egypt.
It replaced the need for clocks that used water.
They no longer had to transport crystal to Egypt.
questions.why: Because Abbas developed a technique for cutting crystal locally, it no longer had to be sent to Egypt.

wrong.A: The technique made crystal more useful, not scarce.
wrong.B: The article says the opposite: they no longer needed Egypt.
wrong.C: Crystal-cutting and the water clock were separate inventions.

questions.stem: Based on the article, why might birds' tails be important for flight?
options: Tails help birds reduce their speed and control their landing.
Tails make birds much lighter so they can rise.
Tails let birds see what is happening behind them.
Tails keep birds warm on cold nights in winter.
questions.why: Abbas blamed his injury on having no tail, which birds use to slow down before landing, suggesting tails help control flight.

wrong.D: Warmth is not connected to flight in the article.

questions.stem: Compared with his inventions such as the water clock, how was Abbas's flight attempt different?
options: It was planned by another inventor.
It was a risky experiment on his own body.
It was done mainly to earn money from the crowd.
It was kept secret from everyone.
questions.why: His other inventions were objects, but the flight required him to jump from a hill himself, and he was injured.

wrong.A: Abbas planned and built the wings himself.
wrong.D: A crowd gathered to watch, so it was not secret.

HIGH.prompt: Some people say that a failed experiment can be just as valuable as a successful one. Do you agree or disagree? Support your position with evidence from the article about Abbas ibn Firnas.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that a failed experiment can be just as valuable as a successful one, and Abbas ibn Firnas proves this well. Even though his flight ended in an injury rather than a perfect landing, he still demonstrated that a person wearing carefully built wings could glide through the air for a real distance, a discovery future inventors could build upon. His own explanation of the failure, that he had forgotten to imitate the tail birds use to slow down, gave future experimenters a precise lesson about what still needed solving. Because his attempt revealed both what worked and exactly what did not, historians still consider his flight part of his lasting legacy, showing that even an imperfect experiment can move knowledge forward.
